etymology: From the old English sooth, “truth,” joined to sayer: literally a teller of truth. The name flatters the trade, for the “truth” the soothsayer claims is knowledge of hidden and future things that God has never given him.
biblical_def: A soothsayer is a truth-sayer — but a lying one. The word joins the old English sooth, “truth,” to sayer, and names one who professes to declare the truth about things hidden or things to come, by arts the LORD has forbidden. The modern ear, catching only the softness of the syllables, may hear something near soothing; the AV means a diviner who trades in secrets that belong to God alone. Scripture never grants him his claim. Balaam, hired to curse Israel, is named plainly: “Balaam also the son of Beor, the soothsayer, did the children of Israel slay with the sword” (Jos 13:22) — his art bought him a grave. Isaiah lays soothsaying to Judah’s charge as a heathen defilement: the house of Jacob is “replenished from the east, and are soothsayers like the Philistines” (Isa 2:6). When Nebuchadnezzar’s dream confounds all his wise men, Daniel confesses their whole guild helpless: “the secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king” (Dan 2:27) — but the God of heaven revealeth secrets. And the LORD’s promise to a purified people is that this trade shall perish: “I will cut off witchcrafts out of thine hand; and thou shalt have no more soothsayers” (Mic 5:12). The believer seeks his LORD, who alone declareth the end from the beginning.
webster_summary: One who pretends to foretell or declare hidden things by divination — a diviner, from sooth, truth.
webster_full: SOOTHSAYER, one who foretells future events or declares hidden things; a diviner, a prognosticator.
From the old English sooth, “truth,” and say: literally a truth-teller, though the truth he claims is stolen.
The soothsayer professes knowledge of secret and future things, which Scripture reserves to God alone.
Balaam the soothsayer perished by the sword (Jos 13:22); the Philistines abounded in the art (Isa 2:6).
The LORD promises to cut off soothsayers from among a purified people (Mic 5:12).
scriptures: Isa 2:6

Therefore thou hast forsaken thy people the house of Jacob, because they be replenished from the east, and are soothsayers like the Philistines, and they please themselves in the children of strangers.
Dan 2:27
Daniel answered in the presence of the king, and said, The secret which the king hath demanded cannot the wise men, the astrologers, the magicians, the soothsayers, shew unto the king;
Balaam also the son of Beor, the soothsayer, did the children of Israel slay with the sword among them that were slain by them.
Mic 5:12
And I will cut off witchcrafts out of thine hand; and thou shalt have no more soothsayers:
corruption_summary: The soothsayer’s trade has not died but rebranded — the horoscope column, the psychic hotline, and the “intuitive reading” are the old divination in new dress.
corruption_paragraphs: This word carries a living corruption, not a mere drift of language. The soothsayer never left; he changed his clothes. The astrologer’s column in the morning paper, the psychic hotline, the tarot spread, the palm-reader’s tent, the phone app that will “reveal your future” for a subscription — these are soothsaying, the identical attempt to wring from hidden powers the knowledge God has sealed. The modern packaging calls it amusement or personal insight; Scripture calls it an abomination and names Balaam its type. That it is dressed as a game does not sanctify it. The question is never whether the horoscope “works,” but by what spirit a man seeks to know what his Maker has not told him.

Set against this the plain law and the plain gospel. The law that names the diviner also declares that “all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD” (Deu 18:12). The soothsayer offers a counterfeit providence: knowledge of tomorrow without submission to the God who owns tomorrow. But the secret things belong unto the LORD, and He has given us instead His sufficient word — “to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). The Christian does not consult the stars; he trusts the One who made them and numbers them and calleth them all by their names.
roots_summary: The word is sooth (truth) + sayer — a claimed teller of truth, biblically a forbidden diviner.
roots_lines: Soothsayer — from old English sooth, “truth,” plus sayer.
It renders Hebrew and Aramaic words for diviners who read omens and foretell.
Balaam is called “the soothsayer” (Jos 13:22); the Philistines were full of the art (Isa 2:6).
Grouped with astrologers and magicians among Babylon’s helpless wise men (Dan 2:27).
The LORD promises to cut soothsayers off from His purified people (Mic 5:12).
usage: In the AV a soothsayer is not a soothing voice but a diviner — Balaam was one, and it cost him his life.
The word joins sooth, truth, to sayer: a man who claims to tell the truth of hidden things by forbidden art.
Micah’s hope was a land with “no more soothsayers” — a people that seeks the LORD and not the stars.

etymology: From Old French sorcier, through Late Latin sortiarius, “one who tells fortunes by lots,” from Latin sors, sortis, “lot, fate.” In the New Testament it renders the Greek magos and the pharmakeia word-group, which binds magic to drugs and spells.
biblical_def: A sorcerer is a worker of magic arts — one who claims to bend spirits, fate, or nature by spell, drug, and incantation. The English word climbs down from the Latin sors, “a lot” or “fate,” through the sortiarius who told fortunes by casting lots; but Scripture strips the trade of its pretended mastery and shows it always broken before the living God. On Cyprus Paul meets “a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus” (Act 13:6), and when this “Elymas the sorcerer… withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith” (Act 13:8), the apostle strikes him blind for a season — the arts that dazzled the deputy could not keep their own master from groping for a hand to lead him. In Egypt Pharaoh “called the wise men and the sorcerers” (Exo 7:11), and they aped the rod-turned-serpent, only to have Aaron’s rod swallow theirs — a counterfeit permitted just far enough to be humbled. Jeremiah lists sorcerers among the lying voices that promised Judah escape from Babylon (Jer 27:9), and the LORD promises to be “a swift witness against the sorcerers” (Mal 3:5). The demonic power behind the art is not denied; it is dethroned. Sorcery is real rebellion, and Revelation shuts the sorcerer outside the city with the idolaters and the liars.
webster_summary: One who practices magic arts by spells, drugs, and incantation, claiming power over spirits or fate.
webster_full: SORCERER, a person who practices sorcery; a conjurer, an enchanter, a magician.
From Old French sorcier, through Late Latin sortiarius, a teller of fortunes by lots, from sors, “lot, fate.”
In the New Testament it renders the Greek magos and the pharmakeia word-group, joining magic to drugs and spells.
Elymas the sorcerer withstood Paul and was struck blind (Act 13:8); Pharaoh’s sorcerers aped Moses and failed (Exo 7:11).
The LORD promises to be a swift witness against the sorcerers in the day of judgment (Mal 3:5).
scriptures: Act 13:6
And when they had gone through the isle unto Paphos, they found a certain sorcerer, a false prophet, a Jew, whose name was Barjesus:
Act 13:8
But Elymas the sorcerer (for so is his name by interpretation) withstood them, seeking to turn away the deputy from the faith.
Jer 27:9

Therefore hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters, nor to your sorcerers, which speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon:
Exo 7:11
Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers: now the magicians of Egypt, they also did in like manner with their enchantments.
corruption_summary: Sorcery has revived openly — the “magick” and spell-craft of the neo-pagan movement, and the ritual drug-craft that seeks “spirit journeys” — and it is the same rebellion the apostles confronted.
corruption_paragraphs: This is no dead word. A generation raised on wizarding fantasy has taken up literal spell-craft: the bookshop “magick” shelf, the online covens, the ritual candle and sigil sold beside the incense, the “manifesting” that is old sympathetic magic under a self-help name. The Greek behind “sorcerer” is pharmakeia — the union of drug and spell — and the modern drug-craft that hunts visions and “spirit journeys” through hallucinogens is that very thing. The world calls it self-discovery and empowerment; the Word ranks its kindred among the works of the flesh — “idolatry, witchcraft” (Gal 5:20) — that shut men out of the kingdom of God.

The apostolic answer was not debate but repentance and a bonfire. At Ephesus “many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19), counting the price at fifty thousand pieces of silver — the converted sorcerer does not curate his old power, he destroys it. The demonic reality is not to be trifled with, but neither is it to be feared, for the Spirit who dwells in the believer is greater than the spirit at work in the world. Christ spoiled principalities and powers openly, and every sorcerer who bows to Him is snatched from the strong man’s house. The city has an outside, and Revelation leaves the impenitent sorcerer there (Rev 22:15) — but the door stands open now to all who will burn the books and believe.
roots_summary: The word traces to sors, “lot, fate” — a fortune-caster and magic-worker; in the New Testament the pharmakeia of drug and spell.
roots_lines: Sorcerer — Old French sorcier, from Latin sors, “lot, fate.”
In the Greek New Testament it renders magos and the pharmakeia word-group.
Elymas the sorcerer was struck blind for withstanding the gospel (Act 13:8).
Pharaoh’s sorcerers imitated Moses with their enchantments, then failed (Exo 7:11).
The LORD will be a swift witness against the sorcerers (Mal 3:5); they are shut out of the city (Rev 22:15).
usage: The AV sorcerer is no stage-magician but a real worker of dark arts — Elymas, struck blind before the deputy.
The Greek word is pharmakeia: drug and spell together, the ancient root of much that is called “magick” today.
Pharaoh’s sorcerers matched Moses trick for trick — until Aaron’s rod swallowed theirs.

etymology: From the Latin carmen, “a song, an incantation,” through Old French charme. A charm was first a chanted formula meant to bind or command; only later did the word soften into a trinket or a pleasing manner.
biblical_def: In the KJV a charmer is not a pleasant companion but a caster of spells. The word comes from the Latin carmen, “a song” or “incantation”: a charm was first a chanted formula meant to bind, heal, curse, or command by the mere power of uttered words. The modern reader, who calls a gracious man “charming” and a bracelet a “charm,” must strip the word back to its old and sinister sense. The law forbids him outright, setting the charmer among the diviners no Israelite might harbour. The Psalmist reaches for the serpent-charmer to picture the hardened sinner, the deaf adder “which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely” (Psa 58:5) — the wicked are more deaf to God than a snake to the most skilful spell. When Isaiah foretells Egypt’s collapse, he shows her turning in terror to every occult prop: “they shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards” (Isa 19:3) — and none of them can lift the judgment the LORD has spoken. Solomon’s proverb mocks the whole art with a shrug: “Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment” (Ecc 10:11). The charm is a chant, and the chant is a lie. The LORD alone speaks words that truly bind and loose, and He forbids His people to seek any other tongue for their safety or their fate.
webster_summary: One who works enchantment by chanted spells — from carmen, a song or incantation, not a mere pleasing manner.
webster_full: CHARMER, one that uses or has power of charms or enchantments; one who binds by spell or incantation.
From Latin carmen, “a song, an incantation,” through Old French charme.
The AV sense is the serpent-charmer and the spell-caster, not the modern “charming” personality.
The deaf adder will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely (Psa 58:5).
Egypt in her ruin sought to the charmers and the wizards, and found no help (Isa 19:3).
scriptures: Psa 58:5
Which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely.
Isa 19:3

And the spirit of Egypt shall fail in the midst thereof; and I will destroy the counsel thereof: and they shall seek to the idols, and to the charmers, and to them that have familiar spirits, and to the wizards.
Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better.
For all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD: and because of these abominations the LORD thy God doth drive them out from before thee.
corruption_summary: Two shifts meet here: the innocent drift by which “charming” came to mean merely delightful, and the live revival of literal spell-craft — love-spells, “spell jars,” and word-magic — that is the AV’s charmer come again.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift is easy to name: from a chanted spell (carmen) the word softened to a locket on a bracelet, and then to a pleasant manner, so that we call a winsome man charming and mean no witchcraft at all. But under that softening the old thing has resurfaced with a vengeance. The neo-pagan revival peddles literal charms: the love-spell to bind another’s will, the “spell jar” buried by the door, the whispered affirmation that claims to bend reality by the power of the spoken word. This is carmen exactly — binding by incantation — and the AV forbids it as an abomination, whatever gentle name it now wears.

Scripture answers the charm with the word of God, the only utterance that truly binds and looses. The law that names a charmer among the forbidden also declares that “all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD” (Deu 18:12), and Isaiah recalls the seeker to the sufficient testimony: “to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). The believer needs no spell to secure love, safety, or tomorrow; he has a Father who hears prayer and a Christ whose bare word stilled the sea. To reach for a charm is to distrust that word and to court the very powers Christ came to destroy. The serpent bites without enchantment, and the charmer perishes with his song.
roots_summary: The word is carmen, “a song, incantation” — a caster of spells, not a delightful companion.
roots_lines: Charmer — from Latin carmen, “a song, an incantation.”
A charm was first a chanted formula to bind or command, kin to the enchanter’s art.
The serpent-charmer stands behind the imagery of the deaf adder (Psa 58:5).
Egypt in her fall sought the charmers among her idols and wizards (Isa 19:3).
The modern “charming” personality is a softened ghost of the old, sinister sense.
usage: The AV charmer is a spell-caster, not a delightful guest — the deaf adder ignores his charming.
A charm in Scripture is a carmen, a chanted incantation, forbidden to every son of Israel.
Egypt, judged of God, ran to the charmers — and the serpent bit her anyway, without enchantment.

etymology: From the Latin incantare, “to chant upon,” from in- and cantare, to sing. The enchanter binds by uttered spell, close kin to the charmer; the modern “enchanting” scene has lost the dark labour the word once carried.
biblical_def: An enchanter works his art by incantation — the word is the Latin incantare, “to chant upon” a person or thing, from cantare, to sing. He is close kin to the charmer: both bind by uttered formula, and Scripture ranks them together among the arts by which the heathen sought to command the unseen. The law names him in the roll of the forbidden: there shall not be found among you “an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch” (Deu 18:10) — every one of them an abomination that drove the nations out of Canaan. When Jeremiah warns Judah not to trust the counsel that promised deliverance from Babylon, the enchanter stands among the false voices: “hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters, nor to your sorcerers” (Jer 27:9). Babylon herself was the seat of the art, and Daniel was schooled where the king kept “all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm” (Dan 1:20) — yet the captive who feared the LORD was found ten times wiser than the whole guild. And when judgment fell on that proud city, all her spells were powerless: her ruin came “for the great abundance of thine enchantments” (Isa 47:9). The enchanter multiplies words to master the world; the servant of God speaks one word of prayer to the Master of it.
webster_summary: One who practices enchantment by magic incantation — from incantare, to chant upon.
webster_full: ENCHANTER, one who enchants; a sorcerer or magician who uses spells and incantations.
From Latin incantare, “to chant upon,” from in- and cantare, to sing.
He is kin to the charmer, both binding by uttered formula rather than open force.
The law forbids the enchanter among the abominations of the nations (Deu 18:10).
Babylon fell for the great abundance of her enchantments (Isa 47:9).
scriptures: There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
Jer 27:9

Therefore hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters, nor to your sorcerers, which speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon:
Isa 47:9

But these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood: they shall come upon thee in their perfection for the multitude of thy sorceries, and for the great abundance of thine enchantments.
Dan 1:20
And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm.
corruption_summary: The word has drifted to mean mere delight (“an enchanting evening”), while the thing itself has revived in the spell-craft and incantation of the modern occult.
corruption_paragraphs: The honest drift has hollowed the word: we call a lovely scene “enchanting” and forget that an enchanter was a man who chanted spells to bind souls and command spirits. But the live corruption runs the other way, restoring the old sense in earnest. The neo-pagan and “witchtok” revival teaches incantations, invocations, and chanted rituals as literal technique — the belief that spoken formulae can bend reality, heal, curse, or summon. That is incantare, the enchanter’s craft, and Scripture forbids it root and branch, not because the words are silly but because they reach for a power God has forbidden and open the soul to darkness.

The law lists the enchanter with the diviner and the witch and pronounces them all an abomination that emptied Canaan of its nations (Deu 18:12). Against every incantation stands the one word that Christians are given: “to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Babylon, the very academy of enchantment, was undone in a day for the abundance of her spells (Isa 47:9); and the captive Daniel, who used none of them but prayed to the God of heaven, outlasted the whole city. The lesson is fixed: the enchanter’s many words are wind, and the believer’s few words of prayer reach the throne.
roots_summary: The word is incantare, “to chant upon” — a caster of magic spells, kin to the charmer.
roots_lines: Enchanter — from Latin incantare, “to chant upon,” via cantare, to sing.
He binds by spoken incantation, close kin to the charmer’s carmen.
The law forbids the enchanter among the abominations of Canaan (Deu 18:10).
Jeremiah ranks enchanters among the lying counselors of Judah (Jer 27:9).
Babylon, mistress of the art, fell for the abundance of her enchantments (Isa 47:9).
usage: In the AV an enchanter is a spell-caster, not a charming host; the law numbers him with the witch.
The word is incantare, to chant upon — the enchanter binds by incantation, as the charmer binds by song.
Babylon kept a whole guild of enchanters, and Daniel, who prayed instead, proved ten times wiser.

etymology: From the Greek nekros, “a corpse, the dead,” joined to manteia, “divination”: divination by the dead. It names the darkest branch of the forbidden arts, the summoning of the departed to learn things to come.
biblical_def: A necromancer is one who seeks knowledge from the dead. The word is Greek — nekros, “a corpse,” joined to manteia, “divination” — and it names the darkest branch of the forbidden arts, the summoning of the departed to wring from them secrets of things to come. The law of Moses sets the necromancer last and worst in the black roll of Deuteronomy, among the abominations for which the LORD cast out the nations. Scripture gives the practice one long and terrible scene: Saul, forsaken of God, disguises himself and comes by night to the woman of Endor, saying, “I pray thee, divine unto me by the familiar spirit, and bring me him up, whom I shall name unto thee” (1Sa 28:8) — and the king who had once cut off such workers now creeps to one for a word, and hears only his own doom. Isaiah exposes the folly at its root: “when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits… should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isa 8:19). The dead do not serve the curiosity of the living; the redeemed are with their Lord, and the lost are sealed in torment. Therefore the law is flat: “Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God” (Lev 19:31).
webster_summary: One who professes to foretell future events by communication with the dead — a diviner by corpses.
webster_full: NECROMANCER, one who pretends to foretell future events by holding converse with the dead; a conjurer.
From Greek nekros, “the dead,” and manteia, “divination.”
It is the last and gravest name in the forbidden roll of the law.
Saul sought a word from the dead through the woman of Endor, and heard his doom (1Sa 28:8).
Isaiah asks why a people should seek the dead for the living rather than their God (Isa 8:19).
scriptures: And Saul disguised himself, and put on other raiment, and he went, and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night: and he said, I pray thee, divine unto me by the familiar spirit, and bring me him up, whom I shall name unto thee.
Isa 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?
Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God.
Lev 20:6
And the soul that turneth after such as have familiar spirits, and after wizards, to go a whoring after them, I will even set my face against that soul, and will cut him off from among his people.
corruption_summary: Necromancy lives on as the seance, the “medium” and psychic who claim to contact the departed, and the grief-industry that promises a word from the dead — the same sin the law names an abomination.
corruption_paragraphs: This is a living, thriving corruption. The seance never closed; it moved to television and the internet. The celebrity “medium” who claims to relay messages from a deceased mother, the app that offers to “connect” the grieving with the dead, the paranormal show that summons spirits for entertainment — all of it is necromancy, divination by the dead, however tender its marketing. It preys on grief with a counterfeit comfort, and it teaches the mourner to seek the living among the dead. Scripture treats it not as harmless closure but as the gravest of the forbidden arts, an abomination that provoked the LORD to empty whole nations from their land.

The Bible’s answer is both a warning and a hope. The warning is Saul: the man who dabbled in the dead died for it, and enquired not of the LORD (compare 1Ch 10:13). The hope is that the dead in Christ are not lost to a medium’s summons but safe in the hand of God, awaiting a resurrection no seance could purchase. Isaiah presses the question that ends the matter: “should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isa 8:19). What answers the necromancer is never the beloved departed; it is a lying spirit wearing a loved one’s voice. The Christian brings his grief to the throne of grace, not to the tomb, and waits for the trumpet.
roots_summary: The word is nekros (the dead) + manteia (divination) — one who consults the dead for knowledge.
roots_lines: Necromancer — from Greek nekros, “the dead,” and manteia, “divination.”
It names the darkest of the arts forbidden in the law of Moses.
Saul’s night at Endor is Scripture’s great scene of necromancy (1Sa 28:8).
Isaiah rebukes seeking the dead when a people might seek their God (Isa 8:19).
The LORD sets His face against the soul that turns after such workers (Lev 20:6).
usage: A necromancer consults the dead — Saul’s midnight errand to Endor is the AV’s one long scene of it.
The word joins nekros, the dead, to manteia, divination: the gravest of the condemned arts.
The modern seance and celebrity medium are necromancy in a studio — the law calls it an abomination still.

etymology: From Middle English wys, “wise,” with the suffix -ard: a “wise one.” But the wisdom the AV names is stolen and damnable — the wizard traffics with familiar spirits — and the modern hero-wizard of story has the word exactly upside down.
biblical_def: In the KJV a wizard is no white-bearded hero but a capital criminal. The word is simply a “wise one” — Middle English wys with a suffix — yet the wisdom it names is stolen and damnable: the wizard is a man who traffics with familiar spirits and gives out occult knowledge, and the modern reader who pictures Merlin or the kindly sorcerer of a children’s tale has the word exactly upside down. Scripture always pairs him with the medium and always under sentence. “Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them” (Lev 19:31) — to seek the wizard is to be defiled by him. The penalty is death: “A man also or woman that hath a familiar spirit, or that is a wizard, shall surely be put to death” (Lev 20:27). Manasseh’s wicked reign is summed up in the arts he revived — he “dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger” (2Ki 21:6). And Isaiah mocks the whole guild for the thin, ghostly noise it makes, calling men from “wizards that peep, and that mutter” (Isa 8:19) to seek instead the living God. The wizard’s wisdom is a whisper from the pit; the fear of the LORD is the beginning of the wisdom that is true.
webster_summary: A man who practices the occult arts and traffics with familiar spirits — a male medium, not a hero of story.
webster_full: WIZARD, a man who practices magic arts and pretends to occult knowledge; one that hath a familiar spirit.
From Middle English wys, “wise,” with the suffix -ard: a “wise one,” but wise in forbidden things.
Scripture pairs the wizard always with the medium and always under the death sentence.
To seek after wizards is to be defiled by them (Lev 19:31); the wizard shall surely be put to death (Lev 20:27).
Isaiah scorns the wizards that peep and mutter, when a people might seek their God (Isa 8:19).
scriptures: Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God.
A man also or woman that hath a familiar spirit, or that is a wizard, shall surely be put to death: they shall stone them with stones: their blood shall be upon them.

And he made his son pass through the fire, and observed times, and used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.
Isa 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?
corruption_summary: The word has been turned inside out: the AV’s wizard is a condemned occultist, while the modern wizard is a beloved hero of fantasy — and beneath the story lies a real revival of male occult practice.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a reversal worth naming plainly, for it shapes how a whole culture reads the word. In the AV a wizard is a criminal fit for stoning; in the modern imagination he is Gandalf, Dumbledore, the wise and kindly master of a benevolent magic. The fantasy is not itself the sin, but it has anaesthetised the conscience: a generation that adores fictional wizards finds it hard to believe the real thing is condemned, and slides easily from the story to the practice. Behind the entertainment stands an actual occult revival — men who style themselves practitioners, mediums, and “chaos magicians,” claiming the very traffic with spirits the law calls a capital crime.

Scripture will not soften. The wizard is bound with the medium under one sentence of death (Lev 20:27), and to consult him is to be defiled (Lev 19:31). Manasseh’s dealing with wizards is named among the sins that filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and brought the nation down. Yet the law that condemns the wizard also displays the LORD who is wiser than every spirit: Isaiah bids the tempted soul turn from the wizards “that peep, and that mutter” (Isa 8:19) to the God who speaks plainly in His word. The believer needs no secret wisdom whispered from the dark; he has Christ, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” and the fear of the LORD that is wisdom’s beginning.
roots_summary: The word is a “wise one” (wys + -ard) — but wise in occult, forbidden things; a male medium.
roots_lines: Wizard — from Middle English wys, “wise,” plus the suffix -ard.
The AV wizard is a man who has occult knowledge through familiar spirits.
He is always paired with the medium and always under the sentence of death (Lev 20:27).
Manasseh dealt with wizards and provoked the LORD to anger (2Ki 21:6).
The modern hero-wizard of fantasy has inverted the word’s meaning entirely.
usage: The AV wizard is no kindly Merlin but a man under sentence of stoning (Lev 20:27).
A wizard is a “wise one” — wise in the forbidden traffic with familiar spirits.
Isaiah bids Israel turn from the wizards that peep and mutter to the God who speaks plainly.

etymology: From the Old English wicce (feminine) and wicca (masculine), a practitioner of sorcery. The very name of modern “Wicca” is that old word revived; but Scripture knows no harmless witch and no good one.
biblical_def: A witch is a practitioner of sorcery — one who works evil, divines, or curses by pact with unclean spirits. The Old English wicce lies behind our word, and the name of modern “Wicca” is that old term revived; but Scripture knows no harmless witch and no good one. The law is stark and unrepeated in its severity: “Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live” (Exo 22:18) — a sentence that measures how deadly God counts the sin, a treason against His sole right to be sought and obeyed. She stands in the forbidden roll beside the enchanter and the wizard: there shall not be found among you “an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch” (Deu 18:10). So grave is the offence that Samuel makes it the very yardstick of rebellion against God’s word: “rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry” (1Sa 15:23) — to defy the LORD is, in its kind, to practise sorcery. And Nahum names doomed Nineveh “the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms” (Nah 3:4) — witchcraft enslaves whole peoples, and God razes the city that trades in it. The witch is not a fairy-tale but a rebel against heaven; and the only deliverance from her craft is the blood of Christ, who spoiled the very powers she serves.
webster_summary: A woman (or man) who practices sorcery by compact with evil spirits — a worker of witchcraft, never benign.
webster_full: WITCH, a person who practices sorcery or enchantment by supposed compact with evil spirits.
From Old English wicce (feminine) and wicca (masculine), a worker of sorcery.
The law commands that a witch shall not be suffered to live (Exo 22:18).
Samuel makes witchcraft the measure of all rebellion against the word of the LORD (1Sa 15:23).
Nahum calls Nineveh the mistress of witchcrafts that sells nations (Nah 3:4).
scriptures: Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live.
There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.
Nah 3:4
Because of the multitude of the whoredoms of the wellfavoured harlot, the mistress of witchcrafts, that selleth nations through her whoredoms, and families through her witchcrafts.
corruption_summary: The reigning modern claim — that there are “good witches” and that Wicca is a harmless, nature-loving religion — is a flat contradiction of Scripture, which knows no benign witchcraft.
corruption_paragraphs: Here the corruption is not drift but open defiance, and it must be met head-on. The modern witchcraft revival — Wicca, “green” and “kitchen” witchery, and the vast “witchtok” following that markets spell-kits to teenage girls — insists that a witch may be good, that her craft is mere earth-honoring ritual and self-empowerment, and that the Bible’s hostility is superstition or male oppression. Scripture grants none of it. It never distinguishes a white witch from a black; it forbids the art itself, root and branch, because every witch by definition seeks power the LORD has reserved to Himself and traffics, wittingly or not, with the powers of darkness. To bless what God curses is not compassion but rebellion.

The Word’s verdict is fixed, and its remedy is glorious. Witchcraft is ranked flatly among the works of the flesh — “idolatry, witchcraft” (Gal 5:20) — that bar men from the kingdom of God, and the unrepentant sorcerer is left outside the city (Rev 21:8). Yet the same Bible that says “thou shalt not suffer a witch to live” also records witches who lived — because they turned. At Ephesus former practitioners “brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19), and the word of God grew and prevailed. The gospel does not soften the sentence on witchcraft; it offers the witch a Saviour who bore that sentence, so that she may burn her craft not under judgment but in repentance and joy.
roots_summary: The word is Old English wicce, a worker of sorcery — the root that modern “Wicca” revives.
roots_lines: Witch — from Old English wicce (feminine) and wicca (masculine).
It names a practitioner of sorcery, never a benign one in Scripture.
The law commands, “Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live” (Exo 22:18).
Samuel calls rebellion the sin of witchcraft (1Sa 15:23).
Nineveh, the mistress of witchcrafts, was razed for her sorceries (Nah 3:4).
usage: The AV witch is a real worker of sorcery under sentence of death, not a storybook hag or a harmless neighbor.
Samuel weighs all rebellion by it: “rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft” (1Sa 15:23).
Modern “Wicca” revives the very word wicce — but Scripture allows no good witch.

etymology: “Familiar” here keeps its Latin root familiaris, “belonging to the household, a servant,” not the modern sense of well-known or comfortable. A familiar spirit is an attendant demon that serves a medium as its household slave.
biblical_def: The phrase “familiar spirit” does not mean a well-known or comfortable ghost. “Familiar” here keeps its Latin root familiaris, “belonging to the household, a servant”: the familiar spirit is an attendant demon that serves a medium as its household slave, supplying the whispered knowledge by which she divines. The distinction from a mere spirit is exact — not any breath, wind, or holy angel, but a particular unclean intelligence in league with a sorcerer. Scripture treats such a spirit and the one who owns it as a single abomination. Saul, needing a word from the dead, commands, “Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit” (1Sa 28:7), and finds one at Endor. The law makes possession of such a spirit a capital crime: “A man also or woman that hath a familiar spirit… shall surely be put to death” (Lev 20:27). Isaiah exposes the pitiful sound the thing makes and the folly of consulting it: “Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God?” (Isa 8:19). Manasseh’s apostasy is measured by it — he “dealt with familiar spirits and wizards” (2Ki 21:6). What speaks through the medium is never the beloved dead; it is a lying servant of hell, and to seek it is to forsake the God of the living.
webster_summary: An attendant or serving demon by which a medium divines — “familiar” in the sense of a household servant, not a friend.
webster_full: FAMILIAR SPIRIT, a demon or spirit that attends and serves a diviner, supplying secret knowledge.
From Latin familiaris, “of the household, a servant” — not the sense of well-known or comfortable.
It is distinguished from a mere “spirit”: a particular unclean intelligence in league with a medium.
Saul sought a woman that had a familiar spirit at Endor (1Sa 28:7).
To have a familiar spirit was a capital crime under the law (Lev 20:27).
scriptures: Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, there is a woman that hath a familiar spirit at Endor.
A man also or woman that hath a familiar spirit, or that is a wizard, shall surely be put to death: they shall stone them with stones: their blood shall be upon them.
Isa 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?

And he made his son pass through the fire, and observed times, and used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.
corruption_summary: The medium’s “spirit guide” and “channeled” entity of modern occultism are the familiar spirit exactly — a serving demon renamed as a friendly helper.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is both linguistic and spiritual, and both must be named. Linguistically, “familiar” has drifted to mean well-known or cozy, so the modern reader imagines a comfortable presence rather than a bound demon — hence the need to mark this phrase off from an ordinary “spirit.” Spiritually, the thing is flourishing under new names. The “spirit guide” of the channeler, the “ascended master” of the New Age medium, the entity “channeled” in a trance, the “familiar” that modern witches openly claim as a helper — these are the familiar spirits of the law, serving demons dressed as benevolent friends. The friendliness is the lure; the servitude is the reality on the other side.

Scripture strips the disguise. What answers the medium is not a wise ancestor or a kindly guide but a deceiving spirit, and the God who forbids the traffic will judge it: “the soul that turneth after such as have familiar spirits… I will even set my face against that soul” (Lev 20:6). The remedy is the sufficiency of God’s own word and Spirit. “Should not a people seek unto their God?” (Isa 8:19) — the believer is indwelt not by a bargained-with familiar but by the Holy Spirit of promise, and he brings his questions to the throne of grace, where no demon whispers and no lie is told.
roots_summary: “Familiar” is familiaris, “household servant” — the familiar spirit is a medium’s serving demon, not a friendly ghost.
roots_lines: Familiar Spirit — “familiar” from Latin familiaris, “of the household, a servant.”
It is a demon that attends and serves a diviner, supplying secret knowledge.
It must be distinguished from a mere spirit: a specific unclean intelligence, not any breath or angel.
Saul sought one at Endor (1Sa 28:7); to have one was a capital crime (Lev 20:27).
The modern “spirit guide” and “channeled” entity are the same thing renamed.
usage: A familiar spirit is a serving demon, not a comfortable ghost — “familiar” means household servant.
The woman of Endor had a familiar spirit; the law made having one a capital crime (Lev 20:27).
The channeler’s “spirit guide” is the AV’s familiar spirit under a friendlier name.

etymology: The phrase renders the Hebrew me'onen, a diviner who reads omens and marks auspicious seasons and days. To “observe times” is not to keep a calendar but to order life by signs the LORD never gave.
biblical_def: An observer of times is a diviner who reads the omens of days and seasons — one who marks lucky and unlucky hours, watches the sky and the clouds, and orders his life by signs the LORD never gave. The Hebrew word behind the phrase, me'onen, names this omen-craft, close cousin to what men now call astrology: the reading of fate in the calendar and the heavens. The law forbids it among the abominations: there shall not be found among you “an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch” (Deu 18:10), and again, “neither shall ye use enchantment, nor observe times” (Lev 19:26). It was the settled religion of the heathen, and Israel was expressly forbidden to copy them. Wicked Manasseh dragged it back into Judah: he “observed times, and used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD” (2Ki 21:6), and his grandson’s reign repeats the charge word for word — he “observed times, and used enchantments, and used witchcraft” (2Ch 33:6). The sin at its heart is a theft from providence: it seeks in the stars and seasons a mastery of tomorrow that belongs to God alone, who made the lights of heaven for signs of His glory, not oracles of our fate. The believer’s times are in the LORD’s hand, and he reads them in the LORD’s word.
webster_summary: One who divines by omens, seasons, and auspicious days — an omen-reader close to the astrologer.
webster_full: OBSERVER OF TIMES, one who marks lucky and unlucky days and divines by omens and seasons.
The phrase renders the Hebrew me'onen, a reader of omens and auspicious times.
It is astrology-adjacent: the ordering of life by signs in the calendar and the heavens.
The law forbids the observer of times among the abominations of the nations (Deu 18:10).
Manasseh observed times and provoked the LORD to anger (2Ki 21:6).
scriptures: There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,
Ye shall not eat any thing with the blood: neither shall ye use enchantment, nor observe times.

And he made his son pass through the fire, and observed times, and used enchantments, and dealt with familiar spirits and wizards: he wrought much wickedness in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.

And he caused his children to pass through the fire in the valley of the son of Hinnom: also he observed times, and used enchantments, and used witchcraft, and dealt with a familiar spirit, and with wizards: he wrought much evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.
corruption_summary: The observer of times is the astrologer, and astrology is not a dead superstition but a booming industry — horoscopes, birth charts, and “mercury retrograde” ordering millions of lives.
corruption_paragraphs: This word names a corruption that has never been more alive. To observe times is to divine by the calendar and the sky, and that is precisely astrology, which the modern West has taken up again with astonishing appetite: the daily horoscope, the natal birth-chart read for personality and fate, the apps that warn when “mercury is in retrograde,” the choosing of dates by the stars. Marketed as self-knowledge and harmless fun, it is the identical omen-craft the law calls an abomination — the attempt to read one’s destiny in the heavens rather than to trust the God who made them. The heavens do declare the glory of God, but they were never given as an oracle of a man’s future.

Scripture answers with the doctrine of providence and the sufficiency of the word. The times are not written in the stars but held in the hand of the LORD, who alone declares the end from the beginning; to observe times is to steal from His providence a knowledge He has not granted. Manasseh observed times and filled Jerusalem with blood, and it did not save him or his city. The believer is told instead, “to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). He does not consult his horoscope; he consults his God, and orders his days by the will revealed in Scripture.
roots_summary: The phrase renders me'onen, an omen-reader who divines by days and seasons — the AV’s word for the astrologer’s craft.
roots_lines: Observer of Times — the Hebrew me'onen, a diviner by omens and seasons.
To “observe times” is to mark auspicious days and read fate in the sky.
It is closely allied to astrology and is forbidden in the same breath (Deu 18:10).
Manasseh and his line observed times and provoked the LORD (2Ki 21:6; 2Ch 33:6).
The sin is a theft from providence — seeking tomorrow’s mastery apart from God.
usage: An observer of times is a diviner by omens and seasons — the AV’s name for the astrologer.
The law forbids Israel to “observe times” as the heathen did (Lev 19:26).

etymology: From the Latin consultare, “to take counsel.” The AV’s “consulter with familiar spirits” is not a modern adviser but the client of the occult — the one who goes to a medium to seek counsel from demons.
biblical_def: The consulter is the client of the occult — not the medium who owns the familiar spirit, but the man who comes to her for counsel. The word is the Latin consultare, “to take counsel,” and the modern reader who hears only a harmless adviser must recover the AV’s dark sense: the consulter seeks the seance, and the law warns that the guilt is not the practitioner’s alone but his. Saul is the great and terrible example. The chronicler writes his epitaph plainly: “Saul died… for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it” (1Ch 10:13) — the crowning sin of a wasted reign was that he consulted a demon rather than his God, and enquired not of the LORD. He had said, “Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her” (1Sa 28:7), and that errand was his death. Isaiah presses the folly on every would-be consulter: when men urge you to “seek unto them that have familiar spirits… should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?” (Isa 8:19). And the LORD Himself vows to hunt the consulter down: “the soul that turneth after such as have familiar spirits… I will even set my face against that soul, and will cut him off from among his people” (Lev 20:6). To consult the dead is to abandon the living God.
webster_summary: One who consults familiar spirits — the client of the medium, guilty with the diviner he seeks.
webster_full: CONSULTER, one who consults; in the AV, one that seeks counsel of familiar spirits.
From Latin consultare, “to take counsel,” but here counsel sought from demons.
The consulter is the client, not the practitioner, yet shares the guilt of the art.
Saul died for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit (1Ch 10:13).
The LORD sets His face against the soul that turns to familiar spirits (Lev 20:6).
scriptures: So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD, even against the word of the LORD, which he kept not, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it;

Then said Saul unto his servants, Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her. And his servants said to him, Behold, there is a woman that hath a familiar spirit at Endor.
Isa 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?
Lev 20:6
And the soul that turneth after such as have familiar spirits, and after wizards, to go a whoring after them, I will even set my face against that soul, and will cut him off from among his people.
corruption_summary: The consulter is not extinct but multiplied — every client of the psychic, the medium, the tarot reader, and the astrologer app is a consulter with familiar spirits, and shares the guilt.
corruption_paragraphs: The living corruption here is that the occult client-base has never been larger, and never felt more innocent. The consulter is the one who buys the reading, books the seance, downloads the astrology app, texts the psychic hotline, orders the tarot spread — who does not practise the art but seeks its counsel. Modern conscience excuses him easily: he is only curious, only entertained, only comforted. But Scripture lays the guilt squarely on the seeker as well as the seer. Saul did not own a familiar spirit; he consulted one, and it is named the sin that killed him. To seek counsel from the dark is to forsake the God who commands us to seek Him.

The remedy is the God who welcomes every honest seeker to Himself. “Should not a people seek unto their God?” (Isa 8:19) — the door He forbids to the medium He throws open to prayer. The consulter is condemned not for wanting counsel but for wanting it from a forbidden source; the same longing, turned to the throne of grace, is welcomed and answered. The LORD who set His face against the soul that turned to familiar spirits (Lev 20:6) sets His face in favour on the soul that turns to Him. Saul consulted a demon and died; the believer consults his God in Christ and lives.

roots_lines: Consulter — from Latin consultare, “to take counsel.”

usage: A consulter is the client of the occult — Saul consulted a familiar spirit, and it is called the sin that slew him.
The word is consultare, to take counsel; the AV consulter takes his counsel from demons.
